summary: SHADOW is health-monitoring software for astronauts on long missions, built for the challenge "Create Health Monitoring Software for Astronauts on Space Missions". It keeps each crew member's own baseline and compares every day against it, across four pillars: typing rhythm and reaction (fatigue), heart, immune system and bone loading. When weak signals from two pillars point the same way, SHADOW raises an early alert, before any single value crosses a threshold. Every threshold comes from NASA evidence or published science, a local AI doctor answers questions with citations, and the link to Earth is encrypted, signed and delayed as it would be on the way to Mars. On a Mars transit Earth answers about 23 minutes later, so the crew has to see problems early, on board.
details:
What it does. On a mission to Mars there is no doctor on board who knows each astronaut's normal, and Earth answers late. SHADOW keeps that normal for every crew member. The demo scenario is day 96 of a transit to Mars, with four astronauts, a crew medical officer and a doctor on Earth. All crew data is simulated. SHADOW is a decision-support prototype, not a medical device: it never diagnoses and never recommends medicines or doses.

Four pillars, one personal baseline. Every value is compared with the person's own median and spread, not with a population average. Each pillar gives a score from 0 to 100 and a state (within limits, watch, alert), shown on a 3D body.

  • Typing (behaviour): fatigue and attention, from keystroke rhythm during normal typing and a psychomotor vigilance (reaction) test.
  • Heart (cardiovascular): night heart rate, heart rate variability, blood pressure.
  • Sentinel (immune): night pulse, body temperature, sleep and a stress index that includes radiation dose and days of isolation.
  • Loading (musculoskeletal): the mechanical load of each exercise session, set against the bone loss expected in flight.

Typing as a fatigue sensor. Astronauts type every day. SHADOW records only when each key is pressed and released and its class (character, space, backspace, enter), never the text. Hold time, typing speed, flight time and correction rate are compared with the astronaut's baseline and combined into a fatigue index from 0 to 100. No extra device and no extra time is needed.

Weak signals that connect. Small deviations that are not alerts on their own (night pulse +7 bpm, temperature +0.4 °C, one hour less sleep, typing 18% slower) are weighed together. When at least two independent pillars agree, SHADOW raises "Possible onset of an illness". When the same signal appears in three or more crew members on the same day, it points to the cabin, not the person. The morning check-in ("how do you feel?") is set against the data, and a large perception gap is a signal in itself.

Three alert levels. The astronaut sees level 1, the crew medical officer level 2, and only the medical officer can send an alert to the Earth doctor (level 3). Each alert shows what was observed, against which baseline, the source of the threshold and a plan from a catalog of 50 sourced recommendations. The packet to Earth is encrypted, signed, waits for a communication window and arrives 11 min 40 s later.

A local AI doctor that cites its sources. The AI doctor answers questions such as "Why has my night pulse gone up?" using the person's own data and 22 official NASA and CSA documents. It runs on a small open model (Qwen3.5-4B, about 3 GB) served by llama.cpp, so no data has to leave the ship. Every answer lists the sources it used, a guard blocks diagnoses, medicines and doses, and if the model does not answer in time the app shows the sourced catalog text and says so.

Solar storm simulator. SHADOW replays the real solar particle event of 11 May 2024 from NASA DONKI. The on-board dose rate climbs, the shelter alert fires for the whole crew, the astronaut confirms they are in the shelter, and the screen shows the dose received and how many minutes the on-board alert came before a warning from Earth could arrive.

Security in the running code. Wearable readings are signed (Ed25519); frozen or impossible sensor values are rejected. Packets to Earth use AES-256-GCM plus an Ed25519 signature checked before decryption. Passwords are stored as argon2id hashes, sessions are signed tokens that can be revoked, every crew route enforces one access rule, and the access log is hash-chained so a secret change is detected. The security code was audited with Claude Mythos: 16 vulnerabilities were found, reproduced, fixed and covered by tests.

Benefits. Problems are seen earlier and on board, without waiting for Earth. Typing gives a daily fatigue signal at no cost in crew time. Every number can be traced to its source in the app (Evidence screen: 169 thresholds, 50 recommendations, 111 engine tests). The same approach fits analog missions, commercial flights and other isolated crews.

Tools, languages and software.

  • Frontend: TypeScript, Next.js 15, React 19, Tailwind CSS 4, a WebGL 3D body, Electron desktop app; also runs in a browser and on a phone.
  • Backend: Python, FastAPI, SQLAlchemy with SQLite, uv; a deterministic rule engine with 319 automated tests.
  • AI: llama.cpp (llama-server) with Qwen3.5-4B, a retrieval index built with fastembed (BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5); for the live demo the model ran on a Google Colab GPU behind an authenticated HTTPS tunnel.
  • Security: cryptography (Ed25519, AES-256-GCM), argon2-cffi, PyJWT.
  • Docker Compose for running the whole app in three containers.
